approvedBy: Draft for review — not approved for publication

cards.headline: Can you sell a product on D-10-2?
body: A store offers to pay a monthly fee.
cards.takeaway: D-10-2 alone does not authorize you to start operating a paid service.
cards.design: One standalone store illustration above the title; no overlapping laptop, coins or labels.

cards.headline: D-10-2 is for startup preparation

body.text: Join OASIS to develop your technology startup idea and explain your preparation activities.
Test prototype features, record user feedback and prepare intellectual property applications.
Prepare to form a startup company and align the business plan with your development stage.

cards.takeaway: Preparation records are not permission to run a paid business.
cards.design: Three clearly separated panels for training, technology and company preparation.

cards.headline: A demo or part of everyday store operations?

body.text: Show inventory features on a laptop and collect feedback while the store continues placing orders through its usual process.
Staff enter inventory and use the program to decide what to order while James keeps fixing errors and providing support.

cards.takeaway: Look beyond installation: check how the program is used in the store.
cards.design: Compare a laptop demonstration with the same program used for actual store work.

cards.headline: Free beta tests can involve different work

body.text: Define the features to test and record users' error reports and improvement suggestions in the development log.
Let the store use the program for real inventory management, with James agreeing to provide continuing technical support.

cards.takeaway: Check the service actually provided, not just the word "free".
cards.design: Use separate document panels for feature testing and an ongoing support commitment.

cards.headline: Test fees or expenses: what is the payment for?
body: Is payment for a fixed period of program use?
Is it reimbursement of actual testing costs?
Do the proposal and receipts explain the payment?
cards.takeaway: Identify what the payment is for, rather than relying on its label.
cards.design: Three readable questions beside receipt motifs, without suggesting reimbursement is always allowed.

cards.headline: Four things to check in the contract
head: Item
Check

body.text: Does the agreed start match the actual installation date?
A monthly usage fee or reimbursement of specific costs?
Are unbuilt reorder recommendations already promised?
Who installs the program, fixes errors and gives support?

cards.takeaway: Even before payment, check the agreed duties and service start date.
cards.design: A four-row contract checklist with clear row separation and wide text cells.

cards.headline: Company income. Your activities still matter.
body: The company's contract and James's own work need separate review.
cards.design: Large central statement and two independent labels; no overlapping decorative illustrations.

cards.headline: Two permissions for different situations

body.text: For activities alongside your current status, review advance permission under Article 20 of the Immigration Act.
For activities under a different status, review prior permission to change status under Article 24(1).

cards.takeaway: Filing an application does not by itself authorize you to start the business.
cards.design: Two sections distinguish additional activities from a change of status without suggesting automatic approval.

cards.headline: Already received a usage fee?
body: Check the date you agreed in the contract to provide the program.
Check when the store actually began using the program with real data.
Check the bank deposit date, amount and specific reason for payment.
Check your status at that time, such as D-10-2, and any separate permission.
cards.takeaway: A later status change does not automatically make earlier activities lawful.
cards.design: Readable timeline of the agreed date, actual use and payment, with the status in force at the time.

cards.headline: Before your first customer contract

body.text: Gather the documents you have: status and expiry details, a startup plan or development summary, and the customer proposal or draft contract.
Ethos reviews the status route and basic conditions, testing versus paid operations, and which authorities or documents need further checks.

cards.takeaway: Document preparation and legally permitted filing require a separate engagement.
cards.design: Separate the documents to gather from the free preliminary review; use the approved office name in the frame.
